column4: Mo thinks he's a nobody. Just a guy who makes tuna melts.
He has no idea that half the houses on this island exist because of him.
This is Mo. Twenty-two years of sandwiches. Same shop. Same apron. A life he'd call... small.
Then, one Tuesday night, while he was locking up, Mo started to glow.
Golden threads. Hundreds of them. And they came with rules.

One: every thread is a life you've touched. Two: the brighter the thread, the more it mattered to them. Three: pull a thread, and that moment never happened. Rule three should have come with a warning.
The brightest thread led somewhere Mo didn't expect.
Theo. Last spring, his very first week on the island. Lonely. Hungry. Counting coins.
On the house. Welcome to the island.
Mo forgot about it by lunchtime. Theo never did.
Turns out, that's normal. In one study, people handed out free hot chocolate at a winter skating rink. The givers guessed it would mean a little. The people who got it said it meant a lot more.
We tend to underestimate how much our small kindnesses matter.
And the thread didn't stop at Theo.

That sandwich was the first kind thing anyone did for Theo here. It wasn't the last. These days, Theo says "Morning!" to everyone. When Bea the baker dropped a whole tower of trays, he was the first to help. And Bea started baking an extra batch for her neighbour, who lives alone.
One sandwich. Three lives.
In a lab game with real money, when one player gave a little more, people two and even three steps away started giving more too. People who had never even met them.
Then Mo found the thickest thread of all. It ran all the way down to the harbour.
Eleven years ago. A storm. A soaked stranger with a suitcase, waiting for the last boat off the island.
We're closed, but... come in. The soup's still hot.
That stranger was Kai. He missed the boat. He stayed. And he built half the houses on this island.
Mo wondered what the island would look like without that one night. Just for a second. So he pulled.
The houses. The porches. The families inside them. Gone.
No, no, no...
Mo pushed the thread back as fast as he could.
There's an experiment about this exact feeling. People wrote about a good thing in their life, but imagined how it might never have happened.
It lifted their mood more than writing about how it did happen. Most people expected the opposite.
Sometimes you only see what something means when you picture it gone.
By sunrise, the threads had faded. Mo opened the shop like any other day.
I never said thank you. So... I wrote it down.
The note was three lines long. Mo read it four times.
And one last thread lit up. Pointing the other way. Toward him.

You'll never see your threads. But they're there. So try this: think of one person who mattered to you, and tell them. In studies of thank-you letters, writers underestimated how good it made the other person feel, and overestimated how awkward it would be.
Mo thought his life was small. Turns out, nobody's is.
